solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A potty essay about old model

indicators.note: the essay sits about, that is around, the next item, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written
a po is a chamber pot, a potty
a thesis is a long academic essay
O is the standard abbreviation for old

explanation.surface: Someone writes off a daft essay on some outdated fashion model.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potty' looks like an adjective meaning silly describing the essay, but it is the noun: a po is British slang for a chamber pot.
explanation.definitionFit: An apotheosis is the perfect example or highest embodiment of something, so it can stand for an ideal model.

clue.text: Teeth needing attention, carries on eating

indicators.note: something eating takes the other item inside itself, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: to ply a trade is to carry it on
to give someone your ear is to pay attention

explanation.surface: A patient's teeth need a dentist's attention, yet they keep on eating regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pearlies' is informal slang for teeth, from their pearly whiteness; 'attention' is the listening kind, not dental care.
explanation.definitionFit: Pearlies is a jocular slang word for teeth, likening their whiteness to pearls.

clue.text: Put head up butt

indicators.note: together with the later word, put up means raised, lifted from bottom to top
put up means raised, and in a down entry raising a word reads it from bottom to top

parts.note: nut is slang for the head

explanation.surface: An instruction to lift your head and butt someone, a playground headbutt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butt' seems to be a verb for headbutting, but it is a noun: a large cask.
explanation.definitionFit: A tun and a butt are both large casks for wine or beer, so the two nouns are near synonyms.

clue.text: Ideology out of this world here in Rome

parts.note: ET, the extraterrestrial, is from out of this world
hic is Latin for here, the language of ancient Rome

explanation.surface: A belief system so otherworldly it seems to belong to Rome.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of this world' looks like praise, but it means extraterrestrial, giving the film alien ET.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethic is a set of moral principles, a body of beliefs guiding conduct much like an ideology.

clue.text: I'm not surprised when sweet is also fresh

indicators.note: something made fresh is made anew, so these letters are formed again in a new arrangement

parts.note: all fifteen letters are used

explanation.surface: Someone shrugs on hearing that a dessert is freshly made too.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder runs from 'when' to 'also', which is easy to miss because it reads as ordinary sentence filler.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a weary retort meaning the news is entirely expected, the same as saying one is not surprised.

clue.text: Two peaches? Or just one?

parts.note: to peach is to inform on someone, and so is to sing
to let on is to reveal a secret, another way to peach

explanation.surface: A greengrocer asks whether the customer wants two peaches or only one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peaches' is the verb, meaning informs: two words for informing, SING and LET ON, join up. The fruit picture is the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A singleton is a single thing on its own, such as a lone card in a suit, so it means just one.

clue.text: Right to cut putrescent nail

indicators.note: to cut into something is to go inside it, so one piece enters the other

parts.note: rotten food has gone bad
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Advice that it is right to trim a rotting fingernail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nail' suggests a fingernail, but it is the carpenter's kind.
explanation.definitionFit: A brad is a thin small-headed wire nail used in carpentry, so it is a kind of nail.

clue.text: Howl about a subdued French celebration

indicators.note: the howl goes about, that is around, the following words, enclosing them

parts.note: hounds bay, a long howl
taken as written
something stilled has been quietened

explanation.surface: A muted, half-hearted cry over some rather damp French celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'subdued' reads as describing the celebration, but it is wordplay; the howl is the hound's kind.
explanation.definitionFit: Bastille Day, 14 July, is France's national holiday marking the 1789 storming of the Paris prison.

clue.text: Immediately remedy catching cold

indicators.note: to catch something is to take hold of it, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: to atone for a wrong is to make amends, remedy it
C is the standard abbreviation for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A call for a remedy right now because someone has caught a cold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remedy' looks like a noun, a cure for the cold, but it is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: At once is a common phrase meaning without delay, a straightforward synonym of immediately.

clue.text: Found answer during meal

indicators.note: something happening during an event sits inside its span, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: lunch is a midday meal
A is the standard abbreviation for answer

explanation.surface: Someone came up with the solution in the middle of a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' reads as the past tense of find, but it is the present-tense verb meaning establish.
explanation.definitionFit: To found a company or project is to set it up, the same as to launch it.

clue.text: Receive broken bones as pretentious drinker?

indicators.note: broken things are smashed apart, so these letters can be put back in a different order

parts.note: to win a prize is to receive it
the five letters, rearranged

explanation.surface: A self-important drinker ends up with broken bones, perhaps after a fall.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is a description by example rather than a dictionary synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: A wine snob is someone who makes a show of superior taste in wine, a pretentious kind of drinker.

clue.text: Bolton regularly heading for Champions League

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals means keeping every other one from the word

parts.note: first, third and fifth letters

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its opening letter, so only the first is kept

parts.note: its first letter

explanation.surface: Bolton Wanderers regularly heading into the Champions League, a football fan's dream.
explanation.walkthrough: Bolton is an English football club; the surface sets 'League' up as part of 'Champions League', but it stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A bloc is an alliance of countries or parties acting together, a league in the sense of a combination.

clue.text: Church's framed art turning up in closet?

indicators.note: a frame surrounds a picture, so the church's letters go around the rest

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
as in 'thou art turning up in', the old form being 'thou landest in'

explanation.surface: A church's painting is discovered hidden in a cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'art' is not painting but the archaic 'thou art', so 'art turning up in' becomes the matching old verb form 'landest in', framed by CE.
explanation.definitionFit: Closet as an adjective means secret, as in a closet smoker, which is what clandestine means; the question mark flags the noun-looking word.

clue.text: Ministerial office uncertain about unfinished flat

indicators.note: uncertain goes about, that is around, the shortened word, enclosing it

parts.note: a chancy venture is an uncertain one

indicators.note: an unfinished word has had its end cut off, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: a plain is a flat stretch of land

explanation.surface: A government minister's office is unsure about a flat that has not been completed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ministerial' points to government, but it is about ministers of religion; 'flat' is the landscape noun, not an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: A chaplaincy is the post or office of a chaplain, a minister of religion attached to an institution.

clue.text: Of an office, to go out to lunch

parts.note: to depart is to go
out to lunch is slang for crazy, mental

explanation.surface: Office workers heading out together for a team lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: The split falls after 'go', not after 'out': 'out to lunch' is an idiom for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Departmental describes what belongs to a department, a division or office of an organisation.

clue.text: In it went — ie the last to score

indicators.note: the answer is found in the run of words that follows, sitting inside them

parts.note: spans the words, dropping the outer letters

explanation.surface: A sports commentator describes the ball going in for the final goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'score' looks like scoring a goal, but it is the number twenty, so the last of a score is number twenty.
explanation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so the last one in a score is the twentieth.

clue.text: Doctor, possibly in drag, taken for a ride

indicators.note: placing something in another item puts it inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a sled or sledge is a drag, something pulled along
the Doctor is a cooling sea breeze in Western Australia, an example of a wind

explanation.surface: A doctor in women's clothing has been conned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in drag' suggests cross-dressing, but drag is a sledge. The Fremantle Doctor is a famous afternoon sea breeze in Perth; 'possibly' marks it as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: To be taken for a ride is an idiom for being cheated or conned, the same as being swindled.

clue.text: Rocket using low gear?

definitions.meaning: second meaning, read literally: putting on casual, downmarket clothes

explanation.walkthrough: 'Rocket' is British slang for a stern reprimand, not a missile, and 'gear' here means clothes, not the engine or bike sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A dressing-down is a scolding; read as two words it also describes wearing clothes more casual than usual.

clue.text: Cane among youngster's plants

indicators.note: something among others is in their midst, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a boy is a youngster
to tan someone's hide is to beat them, as with a cane

explanation.surface: A garden cane stuck among a child's plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cane' looks like a noun, the garden stake, but it is the verb, to beat. The 's means 'has'.
explanation.definitionFit: Botany can mean the plant life of a region, so it can stand for plants collectively, as well as their study.

clue.text: Sisal and other tangled weeds

indicators.note: tangled strands are knotted into disorder, so these letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A gardener's lament: sisal fibre and other weeds all knotted together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'and' joins the two halves of the fodder; it is not a link between definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Horsetails are ancient rush-like plants that spread aggressively, notorious garden weeds.

clue.text: Continue to interrupt very lonely person

indicators.note: to interrupt something is to break into it, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: so means very, as in so good
to add is to continue speaking, as in 'he added'

explanation.surface: Someone keeps barging in on a very isolated person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'very lonely' reads as one phrase, but 'very' belongs to the wordplay. Saddo is British slang for a sad, socially inept person.
explanation.definitionFit: A saddo is informal British slang for a pathetic person with no social life, a lonely loser.

clue.text: Talk about North American

indicators.note: talk goes about, that is around, the next letter, enclosing it

parts.note: to yak is to chatter
N is the standard abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A chat about North America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'North American' reads as one phrase, but North is the wordplay and American alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Yank is an informal, often British, nickname for any American, from Yankee.

clue.text: Girl, one skinny Christian

parts.note: gal is informal for a girl
I is the Roman numeral one
lean means thin

explanation.surface: Describing a slim young woman of the Christian faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a name or a description of the girl, but it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Galilean was an early name for a Christian, as Jesus and his first followers came from Galilee.

clue.text: Dean is holding very soft toy

indicators.note: something holding another item keeps it inside, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: a dean or dene is a valley, as is a dale
B means black, soft on a pencil, and BB is softer still

explanation.surface: A man called Dean clutches a squashy cuddly toy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dean' looks like a name, but a dean is a small wooded valley. 'toy' is a verb, to trifle with.
explanation.definitionFit: To dabble in something is to play at it without commitment, just as to toy with it.

clue.text: Swinging love life described in print

parts.note: bi is short for bisexual, one sense of swinging both ways
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A racy love life written up in a tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the second half, not 'love life': the split comes after 'love'.
explanation.definitionFit: A bio is a biography, the story of a person's life written down.

clue.text: Noise from exhaust? Tread on it

indicators.note: a noise is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: to tire someone is to exhaust them

explanation.surface: A car's exhaust pipe making a racket, and someone told to step on it.
explanation.walkthrough: The car setting makes 'exhaust' look like a pipe, but it is a verb. A tyre is the British spelling of tire.
explanation.definitionFit: A tyre is the rubber ring round a wheel, which has tread on its surface.

clue.text: Hot water is welcome

definitions.meaning: first meaning: an awkward fix or muddle
second meaning: a formal greeting on meeting someone

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a host offering hot water, but 'hot water' is the idiom for trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: A how-do-you-do is informal for an awkward situation, and the phrase is a conventional greeting used on introduction.
